summary: Gus Martins introduces Gemma 4 as Google's open model family complementing Gemini. Open models matter when users need ownership: running on their own hardware, customizing, and keeping proprietary data in-house. Gemma 4 launched in four sizes: E2B and E4B target mobile/IoT devices (E means effective parameters — the models use only 2B or 4B of GPU memory despite having more parameters, with surplus mapping tokens stored outside GPU memory); 26B is a mixture-of-experts model operating in 4B space; and 31B dense is the strongest, running on a single GPU while competitors need 200 GB across 4-5 GPUs. On LM Arena, Gemma ranks 4th and 7th among open models with competitors 2-20x larger. The models support text, vision, and audio input with text output including thinking, coding, and function calling. A key change is the shift from a custom Gemma license to Apache 2.0, eliminating 18-month procurement reviews for sovereign institutions like Ukraine, Bulgaria, and Brazil. Ian Ballantyne then demonstrates practical deployments: agent skills running on phones via Google AI Gallery (iOS/Android), where on-device economics shift from token costs to energy costs and GPU/NPU utilization considerations. For enterprise, the 31B enables replacing 300B+ models needing multiple GPUs with a single H100, A100, or even L4. MedGemma, a medical fine-tune, can serve an entire hospital on 1-2 GPUs. Ian demos LM Studio running the 26B model (~26 GB in RAM) on an M4 Mac with 48 GB unified memory, showing a multi-agent orchestrator farming translation tasks to parallel sub-agents. He recommends getting started via OpenAI-compatible interfaces pointed at Ollama or LM Studio, dropping models into existing workflows, bolstering task-specific evaluation suites, and carefully weighing serving costs including maintenance, uptime, and hardware considerations.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Gemma vs Gemini
sections.summary: Gus introduces himself and Ian from Google DeepMind. Explains Google has two model families: Gemini (most intelligent, hosted, API access) and Gemma (open model for ownership, customization, and data sovereignty). Gemma 4 released the previous Thursday with four sizes.

sections.title: Model Sizes and Efficiency
sections.summary: Describes E2B and E4B mobile models with effective parameters (mapping tokens stored outside GPU memory), enabling phone deployment with full multimodal capabilities. Introduces 26B MoE model (runs in 4B space) and 31B dense model. All support text, vision, audio input with text output, thinking, coding, and function calling.

sections.title: Benchmark Performance and Cost Efficiency
sections.summary: Gemma models rank 4th and 7th on LM Arena open model leaderboard while being 2-20x smaller than competitors. The 31B runs on one GPU versus competitors needing 200 GB across 4-5 GPUs. Models are not the most intelligent overall but are strong enough for practical tasks at much lower cost. Free trials available on AI.dev.

sections.title: Licensing and Sovereign Adoption
sections.summary: Explains shift from custom Gemma license to Apache 2.0, eliminating 18-month procurement reviews. Cites sovereign adoption examples: Ukraine government services, Bulgarian LLM from Gemma 2, Brazilian Portuguese variant from Gemma 3. Notes multilingual fine-tuning is increasingly difficult due to existing strong language capabilities.

sections.title: Agentic Workloads and Model Ownership Economics
sections.summary: Ian discusses the shift to agentic capabilities with high token generation costs, referencing Open Router data showing programming as a top token task. Model ownership lets institutions leverage sunken hardware costs. Models excel at specific modular tasks like refactoring rather than full systems architecture, with deployment thresholds based on capability, hardware fit, latency, and cost.

sections.title: On-Device Demos and Energy Cost Economics
sections.summary: Ian demonstrates agent skills running on phones via Google AI Gallery (built by Coremax team, available on iOS/Android). The model reasons about device actions like triggering calendar and maps apps, accepts images and voice. Key insight: on-device costs shift from tokens to energy — considering GPU/NPU utilization, real-time vs offline processing, and when users plug in phones at night.

sections.title: Enterprise Scaling and MedGemma
sections.summary: Enterprise users can replace 300B+ parameter models needing multiple GPUs with a single H100, A100, or even L4. MedGemma, a medical fine-tune, can serve an entire hospital on 1-2 GPUs with private data under institutional control, illustrating the fine-tuning and self-hosting advantage.

sections.title: LM Studio Multi-Agent Translation Demo
sections.summary: Ian demos the 26B model in LM Studio on an M4 Mac (~26 GB RAM, 48 GB unified memory). An orchestrator farms out translation of the Gemma 4 announcement to multiple parallel sub-agents, each handling a different language, then compiles results into a web page — demonstrating local multi-agent agentic workloads.

sections.title: Getting Started and Deployment Considerations
sections.summary: Recommends using any OpenAI-compatible interface pointed at Ollama or LM Studio with the Gemma model selected. Advises dropping models into existing workflows, bolstering task-specific evaluation suites, and weighing serving costs (maintenance, uptime, capex), mobile constraints (accelerators, RAM), and enterprise infrastructure. Encourages user feedback on fine-tuning and deployment experiences.
